items.stem: Find d²y/dx² for y = 5e^(3x).
items.markingKey: A. dy/dx = 15e^(3x), d²y/dx² = 45e^(3x).

items.stem: The graph of y = f′(x) has a local maximum at x = 0 and a local minimum at x = 2. Explain what happens on the graph of y = f at these x-values.
items.markingKey: At x = 0 and x = 2, f′ changes from increasing to decreasing / decreasing to increasing, so f″ changes sign (R1 R1); hence f has points of inflection there (A1).

items.stem: Tariq writes: "A point of inflection must be a stationary point." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most points of inflection are non-stationary (e.g. x³ − 3x at x = 0 has gradient −3).
items.markingKey: Most points of inflection are non-stationary (e.g. x³ − 3x at x = 0 has gradient −3). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Find the x-coordinates of the points of inflection of y = −x⁴ + 6x³ − 12x², justifying that they are points of inflection.
items.markingKey: f″(x) = 12(−x² + 3x − 2) = −12(x − (1))(x − (2)) (M1 A1); f″ = 0 at x = 1, 2 (A1); f″ changes sign at each (distinct simple roots) (R1).

items.stem: Find the set of values of x for which the graph of y = −3x³ + 5x + 3 is concave down, and the coordinates of its point of inflection.
items.markingKey: f″(x) = −18x (M1 A1); f″ < 0 gives x > 0 (A1); f″ changes sign at x = 0, y = 3 (A1).

items.stem:
Let f(x) = −2x³ − 3x² + 72x − 8.
(a) Find f′(x) and f″(x).
(b) Find the coordinates of the stationary points and use f″ to classify them.
(c) Find the coordinates of the point of inflection.
(d) Show that the point of inflection is the midpoint of the two stationary points.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1 (b) f′ = 0 (M1) A1 A1; f″ sign (R1 R1) (c) f″ = 0 (M1) A1 (d) midpoint calculation (M1) AG (A1) [Total 11 marks]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A curve is concave up on an interval where f″(x) > 0: the gradient is increasing and the curve lies above its tangents"?
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of concave up.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "concave down"?
options: A curve is concave down where f″(x) < 0: the gradient is decreasing
F″(x), the derivative of f′(x); it measures the rate of change of the gradient
Rates of change of two or more quantities linked by an equation, related through the chain rule, e.g. dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt)
items.answer: A curve is concave down where f″(x) < 0: the gradient is decreasing
items.markingKey: B. "concave down" is a curve is concave down where f″(x) < 0: the gradient is decreasing.

items.stem: Explain how the graph of y = f′(x) can be used to find where f is concave down.
items.answer: f is concave down where f″ < 0, i.e. where the graph of y = f′(x) is decreasing.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: f is concave down where f″ < 0, i.e. where the graph of y = f′(x) is decreasing. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why every cubic f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d has exactly one point of inflection.
items.answer: f″(x) = 6ax + 2b is linear with a ≠ 0, so it has exactly one zero, x = −b/(3a), and changes sign there.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: f″(x) = 6ax + 2b is linear with a ≠ 0, so it has exactly one zero, x = −b/(3a), and changes sign there. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The graph of y = f′(x) has a local maximum at x = −1 and a local minimum at x = 0. Explain what happens on the graph of y = f at these x-values.
items.markingKey: At x = −1 and x = 0, f′ changes from increasing to decreasing / decreasing to increasing, so f″ changes sign (R1 R1); hence f has points of inflection there (A1).

items.stem: Find the x-coordinates of the points of inflection of y = −x⁴ + 10x³ − 36x², justifying that they are points of inflection.
items.markingKey: f″(x) = 12(−x² + 5x − 6) = −12(x − (2))(x − (3)) (M1 A1); f″ = 0 at x = 2, 3 (A1); f″ changes sign at each (distinct simple roots) (R1).

items.stem: Find the set of values of x for which the graph of y = 2x³ + 12x² + 4x + 6 is concave down, and the coordinates of its point of inflection.
items.markingKey: f″(x) = 12(x + 2) (M1 A1); f″ < 0 gives x < −2 (A1); f″ changes sign at x = −2, y = 30 (A1).

items.stem: Find the set of values of x for which the graph of y = −2x³ − 18x² − 6x + 2 is concave down, and the coordinates of its point of inflection.
items.markingKey: f″(x) = −12(x + 3) (M1 A1); f″ < 0 gives x > −3 (A1); f″ changes sign at x = −3, y = −88 (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The largest value of f on its whole domain, which may occur at a stationary point or at an endpoint"?
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of global maximum.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an optimisation problem must be reduced to a function of one variable before differentiating.
items.answer: Ordinary differentiation finds rates with respect to one variable; constraints are used to eliminate the others so that a single derivative can be set to zero.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ordinary differentiation finds rates with respect to one variable; constraints are used to eliminate the others so that a single derivative can be set to zero. items.stem: f(x) = −x³ + 12x² − 45x − 1 on the domain 1 ≤ x ≤ 7. Noah says the greatest value of f is at the local maximum. Explain whether this is correct and find the greatest value of f.
items.markingKey: Local max/min at x = 3, 5 (A1); compare with endpoints f(1) = −35, f(7) = −71 (M1 R1); greatest value −35 at x = 1 (A1).

items.stem: A rectangular piece of card measures 58 cm by 25 cm. Equal squares of side x cm are cut from each corner and the sides are folded up to make an open box. Find the value of x that maximises the volume, and the maximum volume.
items.markingKey: V = x(58 − 2x)(25 − 2x) (M1 A1); dV/dx = 0 or GDC maximum (M1); x = 5.44 (A1); V = 3620 cm³ (A1).

items.stem: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the curve y = −2x³ + 18x² − 48x + 8 and determine their nature.
items.markingKey: dy/dx = −6x² + 36x − 48 (A1); = 0 at x = 2, 4 (M1 A1); y-values (A1); d²y/dx² = 12(3 − x): 12 at x = 2, −12 at x = 4 (M1 R1).

items.stem: A rectangle has area 625 m². Show that its perimeter is least when it is a square, and find this least perimeter.
items.markingKey: P = 2x + 2(625/x) (M1 A1); dP/dx = 2 − 1250/x² = 0 (M1); x = 25 so y = 25 (A1); second derivative positive (R1); P = 100 (A1).

items.stem:

(a) Show that the surface area is A = 2(πr³ + 1000)/r.

items.stem:

(a) Write down an expression for the profit P(q).
(b) Find the number of units that maximises profit.
(c) Find the maximum profit.
(d) Find the rate of change of cost when q = 50 and interpret it.
items.markingKey: (a) P = Rq − C (M1) A1 (b) P′(q) = 0 (M1) GDC (A1); P″ < 0 (R1) (c) A1 (d) C′(50) (M1) A1; marginal cost per unit (R1) [Total 9 marks]

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "local maximum"?
options: A point where the curve changes concavity, so f″ changes sign
A line x = a near which |f(x)| → ∞; for rational functions, a zero of the denominator that is not cancelled
A point where f changes from increasing to decreasing; f′ = 0 and f″ < 0 is sufficient
items.answer: A point where f changes from increasing to decreasing; f′ = 0 and f″ < 0 is sufficient
items.markingKey: D. "local maximum" is a point where f changes from increasing to decreasing; f′ = 0 and f″ < 0 is sufficient.

Rafael writes: "If f″(a) = 0 at a stationary point, it must be a point of inflection." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The test is inconclusive: x⁴ has f′(0) = f″(0) = 0 but a minimum; use the sign of f′ either side.
items.markingKey: The test is inconclusive: x⁴ has f′(0) = f″(0) = 0 but a minimum; use the sign of f′ either side. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The maximum value of a function is the x-value of the stationary point." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The maximum value is f at that point (the y-value); the x-value is where it occurs.

items.stem: f(x) = 2x³ + 9x² + 4 on the domain −5 ≤ x ≤ 3. Priya says the greatest value of f is at the local maximum. Explain whether this is correct and find the greatest value of f.

items.stem: Explain why, in an optimisation problem, you should check the endpoints of the domain.
items.answer: The greatest or least value on a closed interval may occur at an endpoint where f′ ≠ 0, not only at a stationary point.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The greatest or least value on a closed interval may occur at an endpoint where f′ ≠ 0, not only at a stationary point. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A farmer in Singapore has 100 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field against a straight wall (no fence needed along the wall). Find the dimensions that maximise the area and the maximum area.
items.answer: 25 m by 50 m (parallel to the wall); area 1250 m²

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "chain rule for rates"?
options: Intercepts, asymptotes, stationary points, points of inflection, and behaviour as x → ±∞
The largest value of f on its whole domain, which may occur at a stationary point or at an endpoint
A non-horizontal line y = mx + c that the graph approaches as x → ±∞, found by polynomial division
items.markingKey: C. "chain rule for rates" is dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).

items.stem: A student claims: "If dV/dt is constant then dr/dt is constant for a sphere." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(4πr²) depends on r, so it changes as the sphere grows.
items.markingKey: dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(4πr²) depends on r, so it changes as the sphere grows. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Gas is pumped into a spherical balloon at a constant 18 cm³ s⁻¹. Explain why the radius grows faster when r = 4 cm than when r = 10 cm, supporting your answer with calculations.
items.markingKey: dr/dt = 18/(4πr²) (M1 A1); decreases as r increases (R1); values 9/(32π) at r = 4, 9/(200π) at r = 10 (A1).

items.stem: A ladder 5 m long leans against a vertical wall. The foot of the ladder slides away from the wall at 0.4 m s⁻¹. Find the rate at which the top of the ladder is sliding down the wall when the foot is 3 m from the wall.
The side of a square metal plate expands at 2 mm per minute when heated. Find the rate of increase of its area when the side is 100 mm.
items.markingKey: A = s², dA/ds = 2s (A1); dA/dt = 2(100)(2) (M1 A1) = 400 mm² min⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem:

(a) Show that, when the depth of water is h cm, the volume is V = πh³/12.

items.answer: (a) shown (b) 12/(25π) cm s⁻¹ (c) 6/(25π) cm s⁻¹ (d) dh/dt = (dV/dt)/(πr²); the surface area grows

items.stem: Briefly explain why you should substitute numerical values only after differentiating in a related-rates problem.
items.answer: Substituting a fixed value first turns a variable into a constant, whose derivative is zero; the relationship must be differentiated while the quantities are still variables.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Substituting a fixed value first turns a variable into a constant, whose derivative is zero; the relationship must be differentiated while the quantities are still variables. items.stem: "In related rates you can substitute r = 5 into V = (4/3)πr³ before differentiating." Explain the flaw in this statement.

items.stem: A student claims: "y = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) has a vertical asymptote at x = 2." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It simplifies to x + 2 for x ≠ 2: there is a hole at (2, 4), not an asymptote.

items.stem: Explain why the curve y = x⁶ does not have a point of inflection at the origin, even though d²y/dx² = 0 there.

items.stem: "A graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It can cross it for finite x; the asymptote only describes behaviour as x → ±∞ (e.g. y = x/(x² + 1) crosses y = 0).

items.stem: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the curve y = x³ − 3x² − 24x + 8 and determine their nature.

items.stem: Explain how the second derivative test classifies a stationary point.
